## Abstract

This paper presents a computational scheme for compressible magnetohydrodynamics (MHD). The scheme is based on the same elements that make up many modern compressible gas dynamics codes: a high-resolution upwinding based on an approximate Riemann solver for MHD and limited reconstruction; an optimally smoothing multi-stage time-stepping scheme; and solution-adaptive refinement and coarsening. In addition, a method for increasing the accuracy of the scheme by subtracting off an embedded steady magnetic field is presented. Each of the pieces of the scheme is described, and the scheme is validated and its accuracy assessed by comparison with exact solutions. Results are presented for two three-dimensional calculations representative of the interaction of the solar wind with a magenetized planet.

## Abstract

The paper presents two contributions in the context of the numerical simulation of magnetized fluid dynamics. First, we show how to extend the ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) equations with an inbuilt magnetic field divergence cleaning mechanism in such a way that the resulting model is consistent with the second law of thermodynamics. As a byproduct of these derivations, we show that not all of the commonly used divergence cleaning extensions of the ideal MHD equations are thermodynamically consistent. Secondly, we present a numerical scheme obtained by constructing a specific finite volume discretization that is consistent with the discrete thermodynamic entropy. It includes a mechanism to control the discrete divergence error of the magnetic field by construction and is Galilean invariant. We implement the new high-order MHD solver in the adaptive mesh refinement code FLASH where we compare the divergence cleaning efficiency to the constrained transport solver available in FLASH (unsplit staggered mesh scheme).

L6@P0: The paper presents two contributions in the context of the numerical simulation of magnetized fluid dynamics.
L7@P0: First, we show how to extend the ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) equations with an inbuilt magnetic
L8@P0: field divergence cleaning mechanism in such a way that the resulting model is consistent with the second
L9@P0: law of thermodynamics. As a byproduct of these derivations, we show that not all of the commonly used
L10@P0: divergence cleaning extensions of the ideal MHD equations are thermodynamically consistent. Secondly, we
L11@P0: present a numerical scheme obtained by constructing a specific finite volume discretization that is consistent
L12@P0: with the discrete thermodynamic entropy. It includes a mechanism to control the discrete divergence error
L13@P0: of the magnetic field by construction and is Galilean invariant. We implement the new high-order MHD
L14@P0: solver in the adaptive mesh refinement code FLASH where we compare the divergence cleaning efficiency to

L17@P0: 1. Introduction
L18@P0: Widespread applications of the ideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) equations emerged in many disciplines,
L19@P0: including, but not limited to, astrophysical and magnetically confined fusion plasma applications. The
L20@P0: mentioned applications, usually deal with extreme conditions like near vacuum up to ultra-high density
L21@P0: environments where shocks of varying type and strength are the rule rather than the exception. Hence, the
L22@P0: accuracy and robustness of numerical simulation codes are very important.
L23@P0: Yet, the mathematical model of ideal MHD has some shortcomings that can cause the results to become
L24@P0: unphysical. As neither the full set of universally valid thermodynamics laws nor the divergence-free condition

L26@P0: obtain physically invalid solutions.

L410@P4: A remarkable outcome of the physically motivated derivation is that we obtain a set of equations which is
L411@P4: known to have a number of desirable properties lacking in the classical ideal MHD equations. The system
L412@P4: (2.16a-d) is not only symmetrizable [12] but also Galilean invariant [3, 7, 13]. The non-conservative terms
L413@P4: found on the right hand side were first mentioned by Godunov [6] who investigated whether the equations
L414@P4: of ideal MHD can be put into symmetric hyperbolic form. Interestingly, he found the same additional
L415@P4: non-conservative terms were required to obtain a PDE system that is symmetrizable, he took an altogether
L416@P4: different approach. The formulation of ideal MHD system considered here is often referred to as the eight-wave
L417@P4: formulation, because it supports eight traveling plane wave solutions. As the non-conservative term on the
L418@P4: right hand side is proportional to the divergence of the magnetic field, it is, on the continuous level, nothing
L419@P4: but adding zero in a clever way. Further advantages are that the flux Jacobian has only real eigenvalues and
L420@P4: the right eigenvectors are linearly independent, i.e. the ideal MHD equations in form (2.16a-d) are hyperbolic.
L421@P4: We will further investigate on the importance of these consequences later in this work.
L422@P4: Numerical simulations of this system are known to be more stable than the same numerical methods
L423@P4: applied to the original ideal MHD equations. This has been demonstrated by Powell [7] and numerically
L424@P4: confirmed by others (see e.g. [14, Sec. 6.1]). From the derivations allowing for ∇ · B 6= 0 a new physical
L425@P4: understanding for the addition of the non-conservative terms emerge and it is clear that their appearance are
